newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - United sees more benefits of merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - United sees more benefits of merger.

text.p: share price)
By Jo Winterbottom

British multi-utility United Utilities saw half year profits jump on Thursday and said it intended to give more rewards from benefits of its takeover of regional electricity company (Rec) Norweb in the second half.
"We are committed to sharing outperformance over regulatory targets with all our stakeholders and intend to announce in the second half...a further initiative," the firm said in a statement.

Pretax profits for the six months ending September 30 jumped to 223.9 million pounds ($376 million) from 167 million previously and the company paid an interim dividend of 12 pence, up from 9.27 pence after a special dividend had been included.
Forecasts had been for pretax profits between 220 million pounds and 249 million and with the figures at the lower end of expectations, the shares were down seven pence at 591.5 pence by 1130 GMT.

"The broad numbers are reassuring...but there is a bit of a malaise in the water sector right now, and I would be surprised if I saw the share price go higher," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
The company gave an upbeat statement on the benefits being seen from integration of Norweb, which was bought by North West Water last year to form United Utilities.
"Increasingly it is clear that the Norweb acquisition is outstripping our expectations of its value," the company said in a statement.

It added that proceeds of disposals of non-core businesses should exceed 400 million pounds "by a good margin," and be completed in March 1997, compared with forecasts of 350 million pounds which it made in March this year.
Chief executive Brian Staples said there had been "a tremendous interest in the generating assets...quite a lot is U.S."
United Utilities has already netted 238 million pounds from disposals and sold its Norweb retail business to the Comet Group, part of Kingfisher, for a net 22 million pounds on November 12.
Staples said earnings growth from the company's core water and electricity businesses could be curbed when prices for both are reviewed in 1999.
He warned, however, that a change in capital allowances on long-term assets made by finance minister Kenneth Clarke in the budget on Tuesday could mean an extra 10 million pounds in tax in 2000.
Staples said to maintain shareholder value after price reviews, the company might need to grow outside its core businesses.
That would mean a focus on its Vertex services unit and a new company to be set up in the second half to compete in energy markets, due to be liberalised in 1998.
"It is very much a case of getting (the two companies) well positioned, well resourced," Staples said.
He said part of the moves would aim to have the value of these companies recognised within United Utilities, adding he would have "some reluctance" to seek separate listings for them.
"It is a step that is too early and maybe too far," he said.
Staples added that the company was not contemplating any more acquisitions in the electricity sector.
"No, I do not think so. I think we are well positioned as we are," he said.
